Hammond, Superintendent, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma. My dear Mr. Hammond;- I note your letter of November 21st, regarding Gideon Peone, and that you have given him permission to return home to attend public school as soon as funds for his transportation are received. In accordance with your recommendation, I am forwarding check for $30.00 from this boy's funds, but in sending this money, I would advise that I doubt very much if Gideon will attend school, should he return to his home. I believe it is best for this boy, if his health permits, that he remain where he is now. Gideon's parents live in the Village of St. Ignatius, on this reservation, where there is a good public school, but when Gideon is at home, instead of attending school, he spends most of his time loafing, when he is not driving his father's automobile around the country, and I have no reason to believe that should he return at this time, he will not resume his former practices, but if you think it is best for the boy to return to the reservation, I leave the matter in your hands. Very truly yours, [signature] Theodore Sharp Superintendent Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 8, 1919 Mr. Theodore Sharp, Supt. Flathead Indian Agency Dixon, Montana Dear Mr. Sharp: There is enclosed Official Receipt No. 176119 covering transfer of $50.00 for Gideon Peone. Very respectfully, Superintendent. (MC) Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Dec. 11, 1919 My. Theodore Sharp, Supt. Fladhead Indian Agency Dixon, Montana My dear Mr. Sharp: This afternoon I purchased a ticket for Gideon to his home town, Ravalli. Gideon is very much interested in engineering and I was in hopes that his interest would induce him to remain in school until the end of the year, but the necessary restraint of a boarding school was too irksome and he was dissatisfied and claimed that he wished to return home to attend the high school at his home town or at Polson. Finally I decided that this school would be much better off without his eternal grouch which not only interfered with his own work, but was a rallying point for discontent among his intimates. Very truly yours, Superintendent. EHH:MG DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Flathead Agency, Dixon, Montana. December 2, 1919. Mr. E. H. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Sir: Enclosed herewith is check No. 11700 drawn on the account of Gideon Peon in the sum of $50.00. I request that you deposit this money to his credit. Very respectfully, [signature] Superintendent. Enc. JP DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Flathead Agency - Dixon, Mont. November 14, 1919. E. H. Hammond, Superintendent, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir;- The parents of Gideon Peon have advised my District representative that they have had a letter from your school, stating that Gideon was ill, and money should be forwarded for his return to the reservation. Please advise me fully the state of his health, and if this statement is true. Very truly yours, Theodore Sharp Superintendent. M/R Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Nov. 21, 1919 Mr. Theodore Sharp, Supt. Flathead Indian Agency Dixon, Montana Dear Mr. Sharp: Gideon Peon had a bad cold sometime ago and to avoid complications I transferred him from the Engineering Department to the Farming Department. He has not been sick in bed with the cold and is about recovered. Gideon has applied to me for permission to return home to attend public school and I have agreed to cancel his enrollment as soon as he obtains his transportation home. He did have sufficient funds here, but he spent the $20.00 to his credit for clothing and shoes. Very truly yours, Superintendent. MHH:MG St. Ignatius, Mont., April 16, Dear Sir, The twenty five dollars that I sent to you was for my son Seldon to come home. We are all anxious to see him. His mother is sick and wants to see him very much. Please send him before Easter Sunday if you can. Yours Truly, Mr. Wm Peon St. Ignatius, Mont. St. Ignatius Mont, Oct. 20, 1919, Dear Son, Received your letter and was glad to hear from you. Your Indian money isn't here yet. I haven't any to send you, I don't run the pool hall any more and I haven't any money at all. I am very sorry tho that I can't send it because I'd like to have you here. When you get out of fall I think you will have to stay there a while. I think your tribal money will be here in November. You wrote and told us you were starting home Monday and we were expecting you. I thought you said the superintendent was going to let you come home you have twenty dollars in the office. If he doesn't want you there why doesn't he send you home. The school is no good anyway. Well I will try to go down there if I get the money. I will close with best regards I remain as ever your father. Ans. soon Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Nov. 6, 1919 Mr. William Peone St. Ignatius, Montana Dear Sir: Your son, Gideon, wishes to return home. As he can attend the public schools at home, I have no objection to his doing so, provided you furnish him the transportation. Gideon is at present enjoying good health. Very respectfully, Superintendent. EHH:MG Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 11, 1919. Mr. Theodore Sharp Flathead Agency Dixon, Montana. Dear Mr. Sharp: I am sending you herewith the vacation request to cover the absence of Gideon Peon until September 5, 1919. Gideon has not been very well since his attack of the "flu". Either he, or someone from his neighborhood have been writing continuously to Gideon's father who is very much alarmed at the reported state of Gideon's health. Our school physician thinks that Gideon would be benefited by a change to his home and I have O.K.'d the request. Gideon has been a good pupil. He is an earnest, conscientious pupil in the academic department and in the industrial department. Please see that he returns promptly the 5th., of September and oblige me. Very truly yours, Superintendent April 4 - 19, Mr. Hammond Dear Sir, Please enclose and find $25 in currency for return of my son Gideon. I surely will appreciate to have you send him home as soon as possible, as we are just anxious to have him home again for a visit. And I trust surely you will have him sent at the earliest date. We are having fine weather here and I know it will do him good. Well I hope you will take quick steps in sending our only son home, which will be awaiting. I am Respectfully, M. Wm Brown Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 10, 1919. Mr. William Peon St. Ignatius, Montana. Dear Sir: Enclosed herewith find Official Receipt #131276 for voluntary deposit of $25.00 for your son Gideon Peon. Very truly yours, Superintendent T/enc Mr. Wm Peon St. Ignatius Mont Box 165 Filed 4-9-19 Sergeant Garnet Hammond, Crosman School, Tacoma, Wash. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 12, 1919. Mr. Theodore Sharp, Supt., Flathead Agency, Dixon, Montana. Dear Mr. Sharp: I am sending you herewith the vacation request to cover the absence of Gideon Peon until September 5, 1919. Gideon has not been very well since his attack of the "flu". Either he, or someone from his neighborhood has been writing continuously to Gideon's father, who appears to be very much alarmed at the reported state of Gideon's health. Our school physician thinks that Gideon would be benefited by a change to his home and I have O.K.'d the request. Gideon is an earnest, conscientious pupil in the academic as well as in the industrial department. Please see that he returns promptly the 5th., of September and oblige me. He has $25.00 deposited on our books but will require at least $22.00 additional to pay his way home and leave a deposit to cover his return fare. Very truly yours, Superintendent Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Washington April 1, 1919. Mr. William Peon St. Ignatius, Montana. My dear Mr. Peon: Dr. Kinnear has given me your letter of March 24th., to answer. As I wrote you, your son Gideon is convalescing from an attack of the flu, and that the doctor had placed him on special diet in hopes of bettering him. Gideon has lost weight and since he has not been regular in taking the diet that the doctor has prescribed for him, he has not gained as much as he otherwise would. If you are unwilling to trust Dr. Kinnear to prescribe for him, I have no objections at to your sending for him and I will grant him a leave of absence until next September, providing you make a deposit to cover his railroad fare on returning to school next September. A vacation request is attached hereto. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent EHH:T/enc Hon. Peon, St. Ignatius, Mont. Gideon is not sick. Doctor has ordered special diet to help him recover from effects of flu. Don't worry. Will notify you if Gideon becomes sick. Yours, Hammond W.M. Collett Western Union telegram St. Ignatius, Mont. March 24, 1919. Superintendent Hammond, Tacoma, Washington. How is Gideon Peon. Has he recovered fully? I wrote you a letter but never received an answer. If he is still sick I want to know. Jan. 7, 1919 Mr. William Peon, St. Ignatius, Mont. Box 165. My Dear Mr. Peon: Replying to your letter of January 3, 1919; now that I know you want Gideon to spend money for a sweater, there will be no objection to his doing so. Gideon, with other pupils, is permitted to draw money not exceeding $4.00 per month for spending money. This is a large allowance. Any sum above this amount would encourage extravagant spending; and before permitting, I prefer to have the approval of the parents. Very respectfully, Superintendent Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Nov. 9, 1918. Mr. & Mrs. William Deon, St. Ignatius, Mont. Box 165. Dear Friends: Your son Gideon was quite ill with influenza followed by pneumonia, but thanks to his naturally good constitution, good nursing and the mercy of God we were able to save him. He has fully recovered his health and is working in the engineering department. By extraordinary precautions we have been enabled to keep the number of pneumonia cases down to a comparatively few. Losses by deaths of pupils has been less at Cushman than at any school I know. Dear Madam & Sir: Sidney was quite ill with influenza followed by pneumonia but thanks to his naturally good constitution, good nursing & the mercy of God we were able to save him. He has fully recovered his health and is working in the Engineering Department. By extraordinary precautions we have been enabled to keep the number of pneumonia cases down to a comparatively few. Losses by deaths of pupils was very less at Cushman than at any school I know. Very sincerely, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Sep. 5, 1918. Supt. Theo. Sharp, Flathead Agency, Dixon, Montana. Dear Sir: Gideon Peon and Victor Cordier have made request for application blanks for enrollment in the Cushman School. If you approve of their transfer, you will please take steps to have them get an early start as our school opens today and regular school work begins the 9th. If the boys can pay their own transportation, I should be pleased to have them do so as our transportation funds are very limited. If they come at their own expense, of course, they will have the privilege of returning home for the vacation in June without making the usual return-fare deposit. Should there be any other young people of your agency whom you could induce to enter Cushman at this time, I should certainly appreciate any effort you may make in our favor. Thanking you in advance for your assistance, I am, Yours very respectfully, Superintendent EHH-S P.S. Louise LaMoose and Louie Michel are also desirous of coming immediately. Cushman School, Sept. 23, 1918. Mr. Thompson, The bearer is Gideon Peone, who has just arrived from Dixon, Montana and has enrolled. Respectfully, Lucy N. Smith Asst. clerk Gideon Fox Dr. Kranear, Geo Cushman School Tacoma St. Ignatius Mont. Mar. 24 - 19 Dr. Kanak, Dear Sir, Kindly give me full information about my son Gideon Pron as I want to get him home as soon as possible; for he has not been feeling well since he left, so I wish you could assist me in getting him home at once. I never heard from him for some time I am also something in wrong; for I never gave him my consent to enter that School. And if any sickness kindly examine him as a party came from Tacoma and told me he is very thin and losing in health. And about the quarantine kindly mention it also! I feel worried over it so if you could send him home let me know and I will send the money. for I need him here very bad, as we are old and need him here, as I could send him here to the hospital should he need anything. So I am trusting you will help us in getting him home as soon as possible. We will await your reply. Respectfully, Wm William Peers Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Sep. 5, 1918 Mr. Gideon Peon, St. Ignatius, Mont. Dear Friend: In reply to your request of August 29, 1918, I enclose two application blanks for yourself and Victor Cordier for admission in the Cushman School. School opens today for enrollment and classification, and the classroom and shop begin actual work on Monday, the 5th. Hope you can be here promptly so that you may get a good start and can keep up with your classes the entire year. If you pay your own fare to the school, you will not be required to deposit return fare should you return home for the vacation next June. You will please see your Superintendent Mr. Sharp for his endorsement of your applications. Hoping to see you soon, I am, Yours very truly, Superintendent St. Ignatius Mont. Aug. 29, 1918. Dear Sir! The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." (Act of August 1, 1914.) EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; these children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission from the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse to or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year." (27 Stat. L., 635. See 2 Dec. Comp., 308.) St Ignatius Montana Nov. 7, 1919 Mrs E. Hammond Dear Sir, I will write you these few lines to ask you how Liden is getting along. I heard he was in jail if so I wish you would send him home if he don't get treated right we thought we send him there to learn something but keep him in jail when he can't learn anything we don't want to have our boy get sick as he did last year. If he does get sick please let us know for he has never been very healthy. I don't think that climate is good for him anyway over there! So you know our dear Gideon is precious to us we think whole lot of him. We don't like for anyone to abuse our children so if you don't like his ways please send him home with that money he has got at the office. From Mr & Mrs Peone Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Nov. 11, 1919 Mr. William Peone St. Ignatius, Montana Dear Mr. Peone: Your son Gideon is not in jail, nor has he been for a long while. Because he deserted, taking with him a young boy, he was court-martialed and sentenced to sleep in jail a week, I believe it was. I do not permit the Disciplinarian to keep boys in jail depriving them of their schooling thereby. Gideon has been well since he returned to school. Last week, he had a bad cold and I took him off the Engineering squad and allowed him to choose his job. He has not been sick. I am sorry you think Gideon has been abused. He has not been. As I wrote you, Gideon has spent the money on deposit here for shoes and clothing and, consequently, can not return home until you send his fare. Very truly yours, Superintendent.
